key_works: Y. Jung et al. (2024), *Characterization of Concrete Reference Material for Analysis of Artificial Radionuclides in Nuclear Power Plant Decommissioning Waste*, [DOI:10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e33041](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heliyon.2024.e33041).

title: Decontamination with tenfold less secondary waste
open: For a specified surface and removal requirement, reduce total conditioned secondary-waste volume tenfold relative to a documented process while maintaining worker-dose and release constraints. Count cleaning agents, consumables, and residues.
status: Gels, coatings, and foams already reduce liquid use. Gossard et al. (2022) identify deployment and waste challenges; tenfold improvement is a proposed benchmark.
why: Prevents cleanup from creating much larger contaminated streams.
key_works: A. Gossard, A. Lilin, and S. Faure (2022), [*Gels, Coatings and Foams for Radioactive Surface Decontamination: State of the Art and Challenges for the Nuclear Industry*](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0149197022001305).

title: Representative properties from sparse Fukushima debris samples
open: Infer distributions of composition, mechanical properties, dust generation, and aging across heterogeneous debris from limited samples and remote observations. Quantify where sampled fragments cannot represent unsampled locations.
status: Unit 2 samples were retrieved in November 2024 and April 2025. JAEA’s 2026 research map reports analyses underway and explicitly identifies sparse-sample representativeness difficulties.
why: Supports retrieval, packaging, storage, and disposal decisions.
key_works: JAEA CLADS (2026), [*Decommissioning Science Diagram: FDR-101, Understanding Status of Fuel Debris*](https://clads.jaea.go.jp/en/rd/map/2026/issues/fdr/fdr-101.html).

title: Groundwater restoration without contaminant rebound after in-situ recovery
open: Demonstrate durable groundwater restoration at representative uranium-recovery sites, including contaminants remobilized from low-permeability zones after treatment ends. Predict rebound and validate post-treatment performance.
status: Studied for decades. Gallegos et al.’s 2015 Wyoming core analysis found persistent uranium in multiple chemical settings and identified redox-sensitive retention relevant to restoration.
why: Protects aquifers and makes closure obligations predictable.
key_works: T. J. Gallegos et al. (2015), *Persistent U(IV) and U(VI) Following In-situ Recovery Mining of a Sandstone Uranium Deposit, Wyoming, USA*, [DOI:10.1016/j.apgeochem.2015.08.017](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apgeochem.2015.08.017).

title: Tailings covers robust to ecological and climatic succession
open: Establish site-specific evidence that tailings covers control infiltration and releases as vegetation, soils, erosion, and climate change over centuries. Identify early-warning indicators and effective corrective actions.
status: Engineered and evapotranspiration covers are established. Caldwell et al. (2022) emphasize site dependence and validation through models, analogues, pilots, and monitoring.
why: Reduces long-term contamination and maintenance burdens.
key_works: T. Caldwell et al. (2022), [*Basis for Technical Guidance to Evaluate Evapotranspiration Covers*](https://www.usgs.gov/publications/basis-technical-guidance-evaluate-evapotranspiration-covers), NUREG/CR-7297.

title: Seawater uranium recovery with favourable full lifecycle performance
open: Demonstrate sustained recovery with favorable material lifetime, regeneration, energy use, marine impacts, and full costs at a stated scale. Report complete balances from repeated real-seawater operation.
status: Investigated for decades. Abney et al.’s 2017 review documents adsorbent and marine-testing progress; industrial lifecycle performance remains beyond laboratory uptake capacity.
why: Could diversify resources while establishing actual environmental tradeoffs.
key_works: C. W. Abney, R. T. Mayes, T. Saito, and S. Dai (2017), *Materials for the Recovery of Uranium from Seawater*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00355](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.chemrev.7b00355).

title: Secondary-resource uranium recovery without displaced pollution
open: Identify residues where uranium recovery yields a verified net environmental improvement after accompanying metals, toxicity, water, energy, and waste disposition are counted. Demonstrate reproducibility across real feedstocks.
status: Laboratory and pilot concepts exist. Kiegiel’s 2018 IAEA contribution studied recovery with accompanying metals; favorable whole-system performance remains feedstock-specific.
why: Could combine resource recovery with residue cleanup.
key_works: K. Kiegiel (2018), [*Recovery of Uranium and Accompanying Metals from the Secondary Raw Materials*](https://conferences.iaea.org/event/146/contributions/5254/), URAM-2018.

title: Population-level ecological effects of chronic mixed stressors
open: Predict chronic-radiation effects on wildlife populations and ecosystem functions after accounting for habitat change, pollution, climate, and migration. Validate causal models across sites and generations using organism-level doses.
status: Laboratory and field evidence exists, but cross-scale extrapolation remains difficult. ALLIANCE’s 2017 agenda prioritizes ecological consequences under realistic exposures.
why: Makes protection and restoration goals biologically meaningful.
key_works: H. Vandenhove et al. (2017), [*The European Radioecology Alliance: Encouraging the Coordination and Integration of Research Activities in Radioecology*](https://researchportal.sckcen.be/en/publications/the-european-radioecology-alliance-encouraging-the-coordination-a/).

title: Internal-dose reconstruction under uncertain biokinetics
open: Produce calibrated individual dose uncertainties when intake timing, chemical form, particle properties, and monitoring histories are incomplete. Validate interval coverage against unusually well-characterized cases.
status: CONRAD’s 2008 work improved uncertainty methods, databases, and guidance. Sparse observations and variable absorption and retention still create case-dependent identifiability limits.
why: Improves occupational assessment and epidemiological interpretation.
key_works: J. W. Marsh et al. (2008), *Internal Dose Assessments: Uncertainty Studies and Update of IDEAS Guidelines and Databases within CONRAD Project*, [DOI:10.1093/rpd/ncn218](https://doi.org/10.1093/rpd/ncn218).

title: Low-dose-rate cancer response and heterogeneous susceptibility
open: Constrain cancer-risk dependence on low cumulative dose and dose rate across tissues and populations, separating dose error, selection, confounding, and susceptibility. Seek convergent epidemiological and mechanistic evidence.
status: Open for decades. The 2023 INWORKS analysis strengthens evidence linking protracted exposure with solid-cancer mortality; precise low-dose shape and effect modification remain research questions.
why: Improves radiation protection and occupational-risk interpretation.
key_works: D. B. Richardson et al. (2023), *Cancer Mortality after Low Dose Exposure to Ionising Radiation in Workers in France, the United Kingdom, and the United States (INWORKS): Cohort Study*, [DOI:10.1136/bmj-2022-074520](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2022-074520).

title: Validated accountancy measurements for advanced solid fuels
open: Establish independently validated measurement uncertainties for advanced-reactor solid-fuel geometries. Demonstrate where existing instruments transfer and where new calibration standards or approaches are needed.
status: Conventional light-water-reactor fuel has an extensive measurement basis. Hu, Hartanto, and McElroy (2024) identify challenges for advanced elements; representative experimental validation remains necessary.
why: Integrates credible verification into advanced-reactor development.
key_works: J. Hu, D. Hartanto, and R. McElroy (2024), [*Identify Technical Challenges in Safeguards Measurements of Advanced Small Modular Reactor Fuel Elements*](https://conferences.iaea.org/event/374/contributions/31325/).

title: Independent verification of declared liquid-fuel inputs
open: Independently verify declared incoming civilian liquid-fuel quantities and properties with traceable uncertainty despite changing composition and physical conditions. Validate through blind comparisons and representative pilots.
status: Hogue’s 2023 study assesses feed-monitoring feasibility. Existing assay principles provide foundations, but qualified performance across proposed reactor-specific conditions remains incomplete.
why: Supplies independent evidence for material accountancy.
key_works: K. K. Hogue (2023), [*Feasibility Study of Fresh Fuel Feed Monitoring for Liquid-Fueled Molten Salt Reactor Safeguards*](https://www.ornl.gov/publication/feasibility-study-fresh-fuel-feed-monitoring-liquid-fueled-molten-salt-reactor).

title: Lifecycle verification of sealed and transportable microreactors
open: Demonstrate continuous auditable verification across factory loading, transport, installation, unattended operation, and return of sealed civilian microreactors. Preserve evidence through operator and jurisdictional handovers.
status: Established safeguards principles apply. Ryan et al.’s 2024 review identifies specific challenges and opportunities; lifecycle demonstrations remain design-dependent.
why: Prevents institutional handovers from creating verification gaps.
key_works: E. D. Ryan et al. (2024), *Challenges and Technology-Driven Opportunities for Safeguarding Microreactors*, [DOI:10.1080/00295639.2024.2372223](https://doi.org/10.1080/00295639.2024.2372223).

title: Verification continuity through repository encapsulation and closure
open: Demonstrate verification preserving credible knowledge of declared material through encapsulation, emplacement, closure, and institutional transitions while remaining compatible with passive safety. Preserve interpretability after direct access ends.
status: IAEA work dates to the 1980s; SAGOR and ASTOR developed substantial approaches. The 2010 report identifies lifecycle implications requiring repository-specific implementation.
why: Aligns disposal with continuing international assurance.
key_works: IAEA (2010), [*Technological Implications of International Safeguards for Geological Disposal of Spent Fuel and Radioactive Waste*](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/geodisposal0210.pdf), NW-T-1.21.

title: Compact surface antineutrino monitoring with demonstrated utility
open: Establish when compact surface antineutrino detectors provide useful independent reactor-state information at acceptable installation, maintenance, and false-alarm costs. Validate over changing backgrounds and extended cycles.
status: Reactor antineutrino detection is established. Neutrinos-Angra’s 2024 on/off analysis reports preliminary surface-detector evidence; sustained verification utility and cost comparison remain open.
why: Could add an independent observation channel for civilian reactors.
key_works: E. Kemp et al. (2024), *Results from ON-OFF Analysis of the Neutrinos-Angra Detector*, [arXiv:2407.20397](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.20397).

title: Quantitative spent-fuel tomography with transferable uncertainty
open: Produce calibrated uncertainty for spent-fuel tomography across geometry, attenuation, irradiation history, and image quality. Validate independent measurements under conditions unlike calibration cases.
status: Passive gamma-emission tomography is established. Choi et al.’s 2024 YSECT evaluation advances an instrument; transferable uncertainty and generalization remain distinct targets.
why: Improves reliability and interpretation of nondestructive verification.
key_works: H.-J. Choi et al. (2024), *Performance Evaluation of Yonsei Single-photon Emission Computed Tomography (YSECT) for Partial-defect Inspection within PWR-type Spent Nuclear Fuel*, [DOI:10.1016/j.net.2024.06.009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.net.2024.06.009).

title: Resilient remote verification across data and equipment transitions
open: Preserve authenticated, interpretable verification records through connectivity losses, sensor replacements, software migrations, and mixed data-transfer methods. Demonstrate auditable recovery with bounded workload.
status: Remote systems operate extensively. IAEA’s January 2026 programme records deployed tools alongside unfinished interoperability and network modernization.
why: Supports growing workloads without proportional travel and manual review.
key_works: IAEA (2026), [*Development and Implementation Support Programme for Nuclear Verification 2026–2027*](https://www.bnl.gov/ispo/docs/dis-programme.pdf), STR-409, SGTS-018.

title: Reference materials and blind comparisons for evolving safeguards assays
open: Supply certified reference materials and independent benchmarks for assay attributes inadequately represented by existing standards. Track bias and uncertainty calibration as instruments and laboratories change.
status: Extensive quality-control systems exist. IAEA’s 2026–2027 programme requests additional reference materials, certification support, and analytical capacity.
why: Makes measurements comparable and precision claims testable.
key_works: IAEA (2026), [*Development and Implementation Support Programme for Nuclear Verification 2026–2027*](https://www.bnl.gov/ispo/docs/dis-programme.pdf), STR-409, SGAS-001–003.

title: Durable consent through successive waste-siting decisions
open: Implement consent processes with independently funded advice, explicit authority, and agreed withdrawal and renegotiation rules. Evaluate informed participation and legitimacy across elections and generational turnover.
status: Decades of siting experience include workable approaches and failures. DOE’s 2023 update supplies a staged interim-storage process; durable transfer across programmes remains unresolved.
why: Enables legitimate decisions about long-lived shared obligations.
key_works: U.S. DOE (2023), [*Consent-Based Siting Process for Federal Consolidated Interim Storage of Spent Nuclear Fuel*](https://www.energy.gov/ne/us-department-energy-consent-based-siting-process-federal-consolidated-interim-storage-spent).

title: Indigenous authority over knowledge and participation in waste decisions
open: Establish funded, enforceable arrangements giving affected Indigenous peoples control over knowledge sharing and influence through their own institutions. Assess community-chosen outcomes, knowledge protection, and continuing decision capacity.
status: NWMO’s 2020 policy commits to community-directed sharing, intellectual-property protection, and support. Durable, independently assessable implementation remains programme-specific.
why: Supports legitimate stewardship and prevents extractive participation practices.
key_works: NWMO (2020), [*Indigenous Knowledge Policy*](https://www.nwmo.ca/-/media/Reports-MASTER/Policy-documents/2020-07-Indigenous-Knowledge-Policy.ashx?sc_lang=en).

title: Intergenerational repository records that remain interpretable
open: Preserve essential repository knowledge through language change, media obsolescence, organizational replacement, and custodianship interruptions. Demonstrate complementary mechanisms and funded testing of accessibility and meaning.
status: NEA’s RK&M initiative ran during 2011–2018 and reported in 2019. Essential-record approaches exist, but uninterrupted understanding over required timescales remains unguaranteed.
why: Supports future land use, oversight, and institutional succession.
key_works: NEA (2019), [*Preservation of Records, Knowledge and Memory Across Generations: Final Report of the RK&M Initiative*](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/preservation-of-records-knowledge-and-memory-rk-m-across-generations_50292bbb-en.html).

title: Waste-management funds resilient to long-horizon uncertainty
open: Establish financing rules maintaining adequate resources as schedules, liabilities, investment returns, and contributing institutions change. Demonstrate transparent stress tests, enforceable adjustments, and explicit residual-risk allocation.
status: Dedicated funds and levies exist. NEA’s 2021 report develops an adaptive framework with country examples; robust implementation must accommodate changing long-horizon conditions.
why: Limits avoidable transfers of current obligations to future taxpayers.
key_works: OECD/NEA (2021), *Ensuring the Adequacy of Funding Arrangements for Decommissioning and Radioactive Waste Management*, [DOI:10.1787/6b316bb6-en](https://doi.org/10.1787/6b316bb6-en).

title: Liability continuity after operator exit or insolvency
open: Keep decommissioning and waste obligations financed and legally assigned through insolvency, restructuring, asset transfer, or cessation of sales. Establish who pays shortfalls and how funds remain accessible after operator disappearance.
status: Financial assurance mechanisms address parts of the problem. NEA/OECD’s 2016 assessment emphasizes early provisions, changing markets, and residual liabilities; exposure varies across jurisdictions.
why: Prevents orphaned environmental obligations.
key_works: NEA/OECD (2016), *Financing the Decommissioning of Nuclear Facilities*, [DOI:10.1787/9789264265325-en](https://doi.org/10.1787/9789264265325-en).

title: Durable multinational repository institutions
open: Implement willing-host multinational disposal with enforceable ownership, cost, responsibility, decision-right, and withdrawal arrangements. Test resilience to government change and unequal inventories.
status: Studied for decades. IAEA’s 2004 framework describes scenarios and infrastructure requirements; broadly reproducible operating institutions for shared disposal remain unrealized.
why: Could expand disposal options for countries with small inventories.
key_works: IAEA (2004), [*Developing Multinational Radioactive Waste Repositories: Infrastructural Framework and Scenarios of Cooperation*](https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/te_1413_web.pdf), TECDOC-1413.

title: Cross-border compensation gaps after nuclear accidents
open: Establish compatible arrangements for timely compensation across borders, including states participating in different liability instruments. Resolve jurisdiction, claim recognition, coverage, and supplementary funding through agreed institutions.
status: Conventions provide substantial legal machinery. INLEX’s continuing work, discussed at IAEA’s 2026 transport conference, seeks broader adherence and effective national frameworks.
why: Makes responsibility and access to remedy predictable.
key_works: D. McCauley et al. (2026), [*The International Regime for Nuclear Liability: A Key Element of the Legal Framework for the Transport of Nuclear and Radioactive Material*](https://conferences.iaea.org/event/421/contributions/38042/).

title: Protected independent nuclear oversight during armed conflict
open: Secure agreements and sustained resources preserving independent oversight, staff access, reporting, and institutional responsibility when civilian facilities face armed conflict. Demonstrate effective protections during disrupted governance and staff rotations.
status: IAEA missions provide operational experience. Its February 2025 Ukraine report documents continuing presence alongside access restrictions and endangered or delayed rotations.
why: Supports civilian protection and trustworthy crisis information.
key_works: IAEA (2025), [*Nuclear Safety, Security and Safeguards in Ukraine: Report by the Director General*](https://www.iaea.org/sites/default/files/documents/gov2025-11.pdf), GOV/2025/11.

title: Predictable funding for independent safeguards capability
open: Provide stable resources for safeguards research, laboratory renewal, training, and deployment as civilian facilities grow and diversify. Maintain transparent priorities and continuity when voluntary support changes.
status: Regular budgets and national programmes finance substantial work. GAO’s 2024 assessment identifies funding restrictions, sector growth, and novel facilities as constraints.
why: Keeps verification capability aligned with infrastructure.
key_works: U.S. GAO (2024), [*Nuclear Nonproliferation: Efforts Are Underway to Address Factors Affecting the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Safeguards Program*](https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-106296), GAO-24-106296.

title: Decommissioning expertise and research access across generations
open: Maintain specialist capabilities through long gaps between projects, including representative materials, laboratories, and practical training. Demonstrate succession and access for programmes unable to sustain every facility independently.
status: Training networks and shared facilities provide support. IAEA’s 2022 guidance addresses staffing needs; project-based employment and uneven laboratory access require continuing investment.
why: Prevents knowledge loss from delaying dismantling and cleanup.
key_works: IAEA (2022), [*Training and Human Resource Considerations for Nuclear Facility Decommissioning*](https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/PUB1959_web.pdf), NG-T-2.3, Rev. 1.

title: Fission barriers with calibrated predictive uncertainty
open: Predict barrier heights and competing fission paths for previously unmeasured actinides, with uncertainty intervals that achieve their stated coverage against subsequent measurements. Separate uncertainty in the nuclear interaction from collective-coordinate and numerical errors.
status: Decades of energy-density-functional calculations reproduce substantial systematics. Predictive extrapolation remains limited, and agreement among similarly fitted functionals is insufficient validation.
why: Reliable barriers underpin fission probabilities for fuels whose differential data are sparse.
key_works: N. Schunck and L. M. Robledo (2016), *Microscopic Theory of Nuclear Fission: A Review*, [arXiv:1511.07517](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.07517).

title: Convergent selection of fission collective coordinates
open: Establish an error-controlled rule for choosing deformation, neck, pairing, and intrinsic coordinates in a reduced fission calculation. Demonstrate convergence of observable distributions when omitted coordinates are restored.
status: The issue predates modern density-functional calculations and remains explicit in the 2020 fission-theory roadmap. Successful fits using a few coordinates do not establish that the reduction preserves all relevant branches.
why: An adequacy criterion would distinguish physical predictions from artifacts of a chosen shape space.
key_works: M. Bender et al. (2020), *Future of Nuclear Fission Theory*, [arXiv:2005.10216](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.10216).

title: Collective inertia beyond the cranking approximation
open: Compute fully self-consistent collective inertias, including residual response and time-odd fields, throughout multidimensional fission paths. Quantify how much widely used cranking approximations bias lifetimes and branching probabilities.
status: Washiyama, Hinohara, and Nakatsukasa’s 2021 finite-amplitude approach made local response calculations feasible in large spaces. A systematically validated multidimensional replacement for approximate inertia prescriptions remains a research target.
why: Small inertia changes can produce large changes in tunneling lifetimes.
key_works: K. Washiyama, N. Hinohara, and T. Nakatsukasa (2021), *Finite-amplitude method for collective inertia in spontaneous fission*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.103.014306](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.103.014306).

title: Dynamical pairing along the fission tunneling path
open: Predict when pairing fluctuations redirect the least-action path, including separate neutron and proton pairing and their coupling to deformation. Validate lifetime changes across isotopic chains without isotope-specific adjustment.
status: Pairing has long been implicated in fission inertia. Zdeb et al. (2025) reproduced fermium half-lives using quadrupole and pairing coordinates; extension to richer coordinate spaces and odd nuclei remains incomplete.
why: Pairing controls whether otherwise similar nuclei have radically different fission lifetimes.
key_works: A. Zdeb et al. (2025), *Microscopic pairing in fission dynamics*, [arXiv:2507.00664](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.00664).

title: Microscopic capture–fission branching without phenomenological widths
open: Calculate competition between neutron capture and fission from microscopic many-body states with a common normalization, reproducing branching ratios across an energy interval. Identify which missing configurations or interactions dominate discrepancies.
status: Uzawa and Hagino’s 2025 nonequilibrium Green-function calculation added proton–neutron interactions and relaxed a seniority restriction, but still underestimated the experimental fission-to-capture branching ratio by about an order of magnitude.
why: Tests whether reaction probabilities can emerge from microscopic dynamics rather than independently fitted channel widths.
key_works: K. Uzawa and K. Hagino (2025), *A microscopic calculation of fission cross sections with the non-equilibrium Green function method*, [arXiv:2504.01572](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01572).

title: Entrance-channel preparation for microscopic fission trajectories
open: Derive statistical weights for initial microscopic fission trajectories from the incoming neutron and compound-state ensemble. Predict exit-channel probabilities without choosing an initial shape distribution to reproduce measured yields.
status: Time-dependent calculations resolve individual trajectories, but assigning physical ensemble weights remains difficult. Abdurrahman et al. (2026) show that initial octupole deformation separates exit channels with different energies and fragment asymmetries.
why: Predictive trajectory weights are necessary to turn detailed simulations into reaction observables.
key_works: I. Abdurrahman et al. (2026), *Influence of the Exit Channel in 235U(n,f) and 239Pu(n,f) Reactions in Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory*, [arXiv:2607.18511](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18511).

title: Predictive fission distributions for odd and odd–odd nuclei
open: Produce validated yields, excitation sharing, and emission distributions for odd-A and odd–odd fissioning systems, including blocked quasiparticles and alternative initial configurations. Establish uncertainty from the treatment of unpaired nucleons.
status: Bulgac et al. (2025) reported microscopic time-dependent studies of odd-neutron and odd–odd compound nuclei. This resolves a feasibility hurdle; broad predictive validation of probability distributions remains open.
why: Important reactor isotopes cannot all be approximated as even–even superfluids.
key_works: A. Bulgac et al. (2025), *Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory Description of 238U(n,f), 240,242Pu(n,f), and 237Np(n,f) Reactions*, [DOI:10.1103/2k8k-vpng](https://doi.org/10.1103/2k8k-vpng).

title: Converged microscopic joint fragment distributions
open: Predict the joint distribution of fragment charge, mass, and total kinetic energy, including covariances and rare branches, with demonstrable convergence in the number of microscopic trajectories. Validate reactions excluded from calibration.
status: Li et al. (2025) coherently combined 25 time-dependent trajectories for a realistic fission application. This advances beyond mean trajectories but does not establish convergence for all joint observables.
why: Marginal distributions can agree while correlations needed for radiation predictions remain wrong.
key_works: B. Li et al. (2025), *Microscopic model for yields and total kinetic energy in nuclear fission*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.111.L051302](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.111.L051302).

title: Microscopic fission noise and dissipation beyond one-body damping
open: Derive fluctuation spectra, memory effects, and additional damping associated with correlations beyond a mean-field trajectory. Test whether one microscopic description predicts both average energy loss and event-to-event fluctuations.
status: Bulgac et al. (2019) demonstrated strong one-body dissipation in time-dependent calculations. That result does not determine all two-body collision, memory, and fluctuation contributions usually represented phenomenologically.
why: Fluctuations determine yield widths and rare outcomes even when average motion is reproduced.
key_works: A. Bulgac et al. (2019), *Fission dynamics of 240Pu from saddle to scission and beyond*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.100.034615](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.100.034615).

title: Observable-independent definition of nuclear scission
open: Define separation into fragments so that predicted masses, excitation energies, and interactions converge independently of arbitrary neck-density thresholds. Reconcile localization-based and dynamical definitions in benchmark calculations.
status: Younes and Gogny’s 2011 quantum-localization treatment clarified separation of fragment wave functions. A universally validated prescription spanning static, collective, and real-time calculations has not followed.
why: A shifting scission surface can change inferred fragment properties even with the same underlying nuclear state.
key_works: W. Younes and D. Gogny (2011), *Nuclear Scission and Quantum Localization*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.132501](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.132501).

title: Experimental separation of scission neutrons
open: Isolate neutrons associated with neck rupture from evaporation by accelerated fragments, with an experimentally constrained spectrum and angular distribution. Demonstrate that the inferred component survives alternative detector-response and fragment-emission models.
status: The mechanism has been debated for decades. Abdurrahman et al. (2023) supplied microscopic neck-rupture and scission-neutron predictions; discriminating experimental extraction remains the relevant open test.
why: Unresolved components bias interpretation of prompt-neutron spectra and correlations.
key_works: I. Abdurrahman, M. Kafker, A. Bulgac, and I. Stetcu (2023), *Neck Rupture and Scission Neutrons in Nuclear Fission*, [arXiv:2307.13132](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13132).

title: Genuine three-heavy-fragment fission probability
open: Establish whether reported collinear tripartition into three medium-mass fragments is a reproducible nuclear channel, and determine its probability or robust upper limits. Exclude binary-fission backgrounds and detector ambiguities through independent coincidence measurements.
status: The channel remains disputed. Jaganathen and Skalski (2025) predict strong dynamical suppression, with model-dependent upper estimates around \(10^{-8}\)–\(10^{-11}\) per binary decay for studied systems; this is not an impossibility proof.
why: Tests how nuclei choose among competing fragmentation topologies.
key_works: Y. Jaganathen and J. Skalski (2025), *Suppression of genuine tripartition in heavy nuclei: A self-consistent perspective*, [arXiv:2506.22534](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.22534).
aliases: Collinear cluster tripartition; genuine ternary fission.

title: Abrupt transitions between fission modes
open: Predict the isotope and excitation energy at which symmetric, asymmetric, or compact fission modes exchange dominance. Reproduce discontinuities in yields and kinetic energies without refitting each neighboring nucleus.
status: Abrupt changes, notably in fermium, have challenged models for decades. Lay et al. (2024) studied multimodal fission with several self-consistent functionals; robustness to functional and dynamical assumptions remains unresolved.
why: Mode switching limits smooth interpolation of fission data between measured nuclei.
key_works: D. Lay et al. (2024), *Multimodal fission from self-consistent calculations*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.109.044306](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.109.044306).

title: Hundredfold faster microscopic fission with certified errors
open: Proposed moonshot: reduce the cost of predicting fission paths and observables by at least 100-fold while preserving specified accuracy on previously unseen nuclei. Supply error indicators that detect extrapolation failure and discontinuous changes of fission mode.
status: Lay et al. (2024) demonstrated neural-network emulation of spontaneous-fission ingredients. A general validated speedup for complete probabilistic predictions remains beyond that demonstration.
why: Makes systematic uncertainty studies and data-gap coverage practical.
key_works: D. Lay et al. (2024), *Neural Network Emulation of Spontaneous Fission*, [arXiv:2310.01608](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01608).

title: Fragment excitation sharing and quantum entanglement
open: Predict the fragment-mass dependence and fluctuations of excitation-energy sharing, and identify measurements distinguishing entanglement-based descriptions from statistical alternatives. Reproduce neutron-multiplicity trends without empirical energy-partition functions.
status: Energy-sharing prescriptions remain model dependent. Qiang, Pei, and Godbey (2024) connected microscopic entanglement to the observed sawtooth structure, while showing that additional fluctuations affect predicted slopes.
why: Excitation sharing controls which fragment emits neutrons and how much gamma energy follows.
key_works: Y. Qiang, J. Pei, and K. Godbey (2024), *Quantum Entanglement in Nuclear Fission*, [arXiv:2408.07375](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.07375).

title: Origin of primordial fragment angular momentum
open: Determine when and through which collective or microscopic modes fragment spins are generated. Find observables discriminating independent spin generation from correlated pre-scission dynamics before evaporation obscures the difference.
status: Wilson et al. (2021) measured weak final-spin correlations, motivating a post-scission interpretation. Microscopic calculations continue to investigate different primordial correlations; measured final distributions do not uniquely fix the mechanism.
why: Fragment spins shape gamma cascades and isomer production.
key_works: J. N. Wilson et al. (2021), *Angular momentum generation in nuclear fission*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-021-03304-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-021-03304-w).

title: Reconstructing pre-emission fragment spin correlations
open: Infer primordial fragment-spin correlations from neutron and gamma coincidences using decay models with independently constrained uncertainties. Establish which correlations are identifiable and which are erased by unobserved emissions.
status: Stetcu et al. (2021) showed substantial angular-momentum removal during fragment decay. Interpreting final gamma observables as direct primordial-spin measurements therefore remains an unresolved inverse problem.
why: Reliable inversion is needed to adjudicate competing fission-spin mechanisms.
key_works: I. Stetcu et al. (2021), *Angular Momentum Removal by Neutron and γ-Ray Emissions during Fission Fragment Decays*, [arXiv:2108.04347](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.04347).

title: Odd–even yield staggering across excitation and odd nuclei
open: Predict how charge and neutron-number staggering evolves with excitation energy, including quasiparticle blocking and broken-pair configurations. Reproduce isotope-resolved yields across even and odd fissioning nuclei without empirical staggering factors.
status: Verriere, Regnier, and Schunck (2021) demonstrated recovery of charge staggering using particle-number projection. Systematic combination with realistic odd-system dynamics and excitation dependence remains incomplete.
why: Fine yield structure affects individual radionuclide inventories and decay emissions.
key_works: M. Verriere, D. Regnier, and N. Schunck (2021), *Microscopic Calculation of Fission Product Yields with Particle Number Projection*, [arXiv:2102.02346](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02346).

title: Microscopic fission-to-radiation prediction without fitted fragment inputs
open: Couple microscopic fragment formation to subsequent neutron and gamma decay, propagating joint uncertainties without independently fitted mass, excitation, and spin distributions. Validate correlated emissions as well as averages.
status: Statistical fragment-decay simulators such as CGMF already produce event histories. The missing closure is reliably deriving their complete initial fragment distribution from predictive microscopic dynamics.
why: Replaces partly compensating empirical inputs with a coherent prediction.
key_works: P. Talou et al. (2021), *Fission fragment decay simulations with the CGMF code*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cpc.2021.108087](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpc.2021.108087).

title: A common fission clock for atomic and nuclear probes
open: Construct and validate a common time-distribution inference from atomic probes, prescission emissions, and fragment observables. Determine which portion of the lifetime each technique measures, including intervals without particle evaporation.
status: Historical atomic and nuclear estimates differed by orders of magnitude. Senthil Kannan et al. (2018) proposed a dynamical reconciliation; simultaneous discriminating measurements and broadly validated inference remain open.
why: Fission times constrain dissipation and equilibration independently of final fragment yields.
key_works: M. T. Senthil Kannan et al. (2018), *Dynamical model calculation to reconcile the nuclear fission lifetime from different measurement techniques*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.98.021601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.98.021601).

title: Uranium-238 state-resolved inelastic-scattering closure
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Determine the 238U inelastic cross section by consistently combining observed gamma transitions, unobserved cascades, and direct neutron measurements. Close the gap between state-specific measurements and the total channel with documented covariance.
status: A high-priority request has existed since 2008. Kerveno et al. (2021) supplied extensive neutron-induced gamma data; incomplete level schemes and reaction-model dependence still complicate reconstruction.
why: Uranium inelastic scattering changes fast-neutron spectra and interpretation of irradiations.
key_works: M. Kerveno et al. (2021), *Measurement of 238U(n,n′γ) cross section data and their impact on reaction models*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.104.044605](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.104.044605); OECD NEA, [HPRL request](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68811/92-u-238-n-inl).

title: Plutonium-239 capture normalization across energy regimes
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Reconcile resonance-region and fast-energy 239Pu capture measurements within a joint capture–fission evaluation retaining shared normalization uncertainties. Demonstrate agreement with independent measurements without separate energy-dependent adjustments that conceal discrepancies.
status: Mosby et al. (2018) provided a unifying capture measurement from keV to MeV energies. The NEA capture request remains active; improved coverage has not eliminated evaluation and normalization questions.
why: Capture competition influences isotope evolution and neutron balances in civilian fuel calculations.
key_works: S. Mosby et al. (2018), *Unifying measurement of 239Pu(n,γ) in the keV to MeV energy regime*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.97.041601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.97.041601).

title: Independently replicated plutonium-241 capture data
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Complete analysis and independent replication of 241Pu neutron-capture measurements, then establish a covariance-bearing evaluation resolving dependence on the historical dataset. Test compatibility with simultaneously measured competing channels.
status: Weston and Todd’s 1978 work long dominated direct capture information. CEA reported new measurements undergoing analysis in 2026; acquiring data is therefore already a partial result.
why: Sparse capture data limit isotope-inventory predictions involving 241Pu.
key_works: L. W. Weston and J. H. Todd (1978), *Neutron Capture and Fission Cross Sections of Plutonium-241*, [DOI:10.13182/NSE78-A27176](https://doi.org/10.13182/NSE78-A27176); CEA (2026), [*Experimental challenges of nuclear reactions on plutonium-241*](https://irfu.cea.fr/en/Phocea/Vie_des_labos/Ast/ast.php?id_ast=5474&t=fait_marquant).

title: Americium-241 fast-energy capture uncertainty
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Reduce uncertainty in 241Am capture across fast-energy ranges identified by sensitivity studies, using consistent differential measurements and evaluation. Demonstrate improvement under independent validation, including normalization correlations.
status: An established NEA priority before the 2018 n_TOF publication. The thermal-data component was completed in May 2022; the request leaves the fast-energy component in progress.
why: The remaining gap affects inventories and irradiation predictions for americium-bearing civilian materials.
key_works: E. Mendoza et al. (2018), *Measurement and analysis of the 241Am neutron capture cross section at the n_TOF facility at CERN*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.97.054616](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.97.054616); OECD NEA, [HPRL status](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68808/95-am-241-n-g-n-tot).

title: Consistent gadolinium-155 and gadolinium-157 resonance evaluations
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Produce capture and transmission evaluations for 155Gd and 157Gd that jointly reproduce modern experiments and resolve discrepant thermal values. Meet the requested roughly 4% accuracy with independently validated covariance.
status: NEA requests were submitted in 2018. Mastromarco et al. (2019) supplied thermal and epithermal measurements; subsequent work concerns evaluation and validation rather than wholly unmeasured reactions.
why: These isotopes strongly influence gadolinium neutron-absorber behavior.
key_works: M. Mastromarco et al. (2019), *Cross section measurements of 155,157Gd(n,γ) induced by thermal and epithermal neutrons*, [DOI:10.1140/epja/i2019-12692-7](https://doi.org/10.1140/epja/i2019-12692-7); OECD NEA, [request status](https://cms.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68888/64-gd-155-n-g-n-tot).

title: Iron-56 inelastic neutron–gamma channel closure
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Reconcile 56Fe outgoing-neutron spectra, level-specific gamma production, and total inelastic scattering over the fast-energy range. Identify missing transitions or reaction-model ingredients and publish a common covariance evaluation.
status: A NEA high-priority request has remained active since 2008. The 2018 CIELO evaluation improved iron modeling; state-resolved measurements and channel consistency remain active work.
why: Iron is ubiquitous in structural materials, shielding, and neutron diagnostics.
key_works: M. Herman et al. (2018), [*Evaluation of Neutron Reactions on Iron Isotopes for CIELO and ENDF/B-VIII.0*](https://www.ornl.gov/publication/evaluation-neutron-reactions-iron-isotopes-cielo-and-endfb-viii0); OECD NEA, [High Priority Request List](https://www.oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_68746/hprlapp).

title: Oxygen-16 neutron-induced alpha-channel consistency
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Determine a common 16O(n,α) evaluation consistent with energy- and angle-dependent measurements, excited-state channels, and the inverse reaction. Resolve normalization, angular-extrapolation, and resonance-modeling disagreements.
status: This longstanding data need has received new measurements. Lee et al. (2024) measured differential cross sections over 3.8–15 MeV; this does not settle all channels, angular coverage, and competing evaluations.
why: Oxygen reaction uncertainties affect oxide fuels, water, and radiation-response calculations.
key_works: H. Y. Lee et al. (2024), *Differential cross sections of the 16O(n,α) reaction at neutron energies from 3.8 to 15 MeV*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.109.014601](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.109.014601).

title: Chlorine-35 absorption evaluation with measured covariance
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Reconcile new 35Cl(n,p) data across thermal, epithermal, and fast energies, replacing missing fast-energy covariance with experimentally supported uncertainty. Test a common evaluation against differential and chlorine-sensitive integral experiments.
status: Hanselman et al. (2025) improved fast-spectrum averages but identified remaining discrepancies. Martinez-Cañadas et al. (2026) measured the reaction through 120 keV; consistent evaluation is the remaining task.
why: Chlorine absorption influences molten-chloride systems and neutron-detector response.
key_works: K. Hanselman et al. (2025), *Constraining the impact of chlorine as a neutron absorber in next-gen fast reactor designs*, [DOI:10.1038/s41598-025-28299-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-28299-6); M. A. Martinez-Cañadas et al. (2026), *Measurement of the 35Cl(n,p)35S cross-section at the CERN n_TOF facility from subthermal energy to 120 keV*, [DOI:10.1140/epja/s10050-026-01826-3](https://doi.org/10.1140/epja/s10050-026-01826-3).

title: Energy-resolved independent fission yields between standard points
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Measure independent isotope yields densely enough in incident-neutron energy to test interpolation between commonly tabulated thermal and fast points. Resolve changes across multi-chance-fission thresholds and publish energy-to-energy correlations.
status: Evaluations and models supply much interpolation. Liu et al. (2025) reproduced several energy trends with Langevin and statistical modeling; sparse data leave many individual isotope trends untested.
why: Different neutron spectra produce different decay inventories even at equal average fission rates.
key_works: L.-L. Liu et al. (2025), *Energy dependence of fission product yields in 235U(n,f) within the Langevin approach incorporated with the statistical model*, [DOI:10.1088/1674-1137/adb70b](https://doi.org/10.1088/1674-1137/adb70b).

title: Experimentally anchored fission-yield covariance matrices
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Establish isotope-to-isotope and energy-to-energy yield covariance matrices supported by experimental likelihoods, normalization constraints, and documented shared systematics. Validate coverage on withheld measurements.
status: Full covariance evaluations have advanced. Belfiore et al. (2024/2025) demonstrated consequential differences using newer 235U yield covariance; comparable support is not uniform across isotopes and energies.
why: Guessed or omitted correlations can make inventories appear artificially certain or uncertain.
key_works: E. Belfiore et al. (2024 online; 2025 issue), *On the Assumptions Behind Statistical Sampling: A 235U Fission Yield Uncertainty Propagation Case Study*, [DOI:10.1080/00295639.2024.2323217](https://doi.org/10.1080/00295639.2024.2323217).

title: Joint consistency of yields and emitted decay energy
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Evaluate independent and cumulative yields, delayed-neutron production, and prompt and delayed radiation within one statistically consistent dataset. Require conservation laws and simultaneous agreement without compensating errors among separately adjusted files.
status: Minato and Iwamoto (2024) used CCONE to fit multiple observables for thermal 235U fission. Generalization across isotopes and incident energies, with independent validation, remains incomplete.
why: Plausible individual observables can conceal incompatible heat and inventory predictions.
key_works: F. Minato and O. Iwamoto (2024), *Fission Fragment Yields of 235U(n_th,f) Evaluated by the CCONE Code System*, [arXiv:2404.17728](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.17728).

title: Isomeric yield ratios for influential fission products
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Measure ground-state versus metastable-state production fractions for fission products dominating decay-heat and antineutrino-spectrum uncertainty. Resolve incident-energy dependence and separate independent production from subsequent feeding.
status: Mattera et al. (2025) evaluated 43 isomeric yield ratios and demonstrated substantial spectral consequences. Accurate experimental ratios remain needed for influential individual products.
why: Isomers can have different lifetimes, beta branches, and radiation spectra despite identical mass and charge.
key_works: A. Mattera et al. (2025), *Isomeric yield ratios of fission products: A missing piece in reactor antineutrino summation calculations*, [DOI:10.1103/xrgf-6f3h](https://doi.org/10.1103/xrgf-6f3h).

title: Prompt-neutron spectrum tails and reference normalization
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Establish independently reproducible low- and high-energy tails of reference prompt-fission-neutron spectra, including detector-response and normalization correlations. Quantify propagation of reference-spectrum disagreement into measurements normalized to it.
status: The 252Cf reference spectrum has decades of measurements. Neudecker et al. (2025) revisited its evaluation; reconstruction of legacy assumptions and uncertainty remains part of the standards problem.
why: A shared spectral standard can transmit a common bias across otherwise independent experiments.
key_works: D. Neudecker et al. (2025), [*Re-evaluating the prompt fission neutron spectrum of spontaneously fissioning 252Cf*](https://laro.lanl.gov/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/Re-evaluating-the-prompt-fission-neutron-spectrum/9916503075503761).

title: Event-level neutron–gamma–fragment reference datasets
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Publish response-characterized coincidence datasets connecting fragment identity and kinetic energy with neutron and gamma multiplicities, energies, and directions. Supply enough information to distinguish models reproducing identical one-dimensional spectra.
status: Correlated event generators and selected coincidence measurements exist. Talou et al. (2018) documented the importance of correlated fission data; comprehensive reaction coverage remains incomplete.
why: Joint measurements test the origin of correlations rather than only average emissions.
key_works: P. Talou et al. (2018), *Correlated Prompt Fission Data in Transport Simulations*, [arXiv:1710.00107](https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.00107).

title: Time-resolved gamma emission across the prompt–delayed boundary
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Measure gamma energy and multiplicity continuously after fission, identifying isomeric contributions across customary prompt windows. Reconcile experiments with different time cuts through a validated common representation.
status: Prompt averages are measured, including STEFF results published in 2024. Prompt measurements do not fully determine delayed tails or correlations with particular fragments and neutron emission.
why: Time-window dependence affects experimental comparisons and predictions of gamma heating.
key_works: T. Wright et al. (2024), *Measurement of the prompt fission γ-rays from slow neutron-induced fission of 235U with STEFF*, [DOI:10.1140/epja/s10050-024-01277-8](https://doi.org/10.1140/epja/s10050-024-01277-8).

title: Precursor-resolved delayed-neutron emission spectra
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Measure neutron-energy spectra and branching correlations for remaining influential delayed-neutron precursors, including weak high-energy branches. Demonstrate reproduction of aggregate spectra across fissioning systems and irradiation histories.
status: Dimitriou et al. (2021) established a reference database with recommended probabilities and group parameters. It does not supply precise spectra for every relevant precursor.
why: Group averages can hide errors when precursor mixtures change.
key_works: P. Dimitriou et al. (2021), *Development of a Reference Database for Beta-Delayed Neutron Emission*, [arXiv:2102.01165](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01165).

title: Remaining Pandemonium-biased fission-product decays
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Complete total-absorption and complementary beta-spectrum measurements for high-impact decays whose feeding distributions remain vulnerable to missed gamma cascades. Incorporate measured branching probabilities and uncertainties into evaluated libraries.
status: The Pandemonium effect has been recognized since 1977. Algora et al. (2026) report new measurements and JEFF updates while motivating further work; already measured decays must be distinguished from remaining targets.
why: Biased beta feeding distorts gamma heat, electron heat, and predicted antineutrino spectra together.
key_works: A. Algora et al. (2026), *Pandemonium free data for the JEFF-project*, [DOI:10.1140/epja/s10050-026-01931-3](https://doi.org/10.1140/epja/s10050-026-01931-3).

title: Early-time decay heat with separate beta and gamma benchmarks
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Obtain independent pulse-irradiation decay-heat benchmarks separately resolving electron and electromagnetic energy at short cooling times. Identify specific decay-data errors responsible for disagreements instead of validating only total heat.
status: Historical measurements and summation evaluations provide substantial coverage. Nichols et al. (2023) review persistent priorities; agreement in total power can conceal opposite beta and gamma errors.
why: Radiation components deposit energy over different distances and need separate predictions.
key_works: A. L. Nichols et al. (2023), *Improving fission-product decay data for reactor applications: part I—decay heat*, [DOI:10.1140/epja/s10050-023-00969-x](https://doi.org/10.1140/epja/s10050-023-00969-x).

title: Ground-state beta-feeding identifiability
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Determine ground-state beta-branch intensities with uncertainties accounting for gamma-free transitions, detector thresholds, and uncertain forbidden shapes. Establish when total-absorption measurements require an independent observable for a unique answer.
status: Total-absorption methods reduce Pandemonium bias but do not automatically identify ground-state feeding. Guadilla (2024) examines extraction methods and remaining response and beta-shape assumptions.
why: Misassigned ground-state branches directly change high-energy beta and antineutrino contributions.
key_works: V. Guadilla (2024), *Ground-state β-feeding determination using total-absorption spectrometers*, [DOI:10.3389/fphy.2024.1452988](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphy.2024.1452988).

title: Reconstructible experimental nuclear-data likelihoods
subfield: Nuclear reaction, fission-yield, and decay data
open: Make reaction measurements reproducible from machine-readable data, correction histories, detector responses, and correlated uncertainty, including legacy experiments. Demonstrate independent regeneration of likelihoods rather than retrieval of final tables alone.
status: EXFOR preserves extensive experimental data. NEA’s MEDUSAL work, including its 2026 requirements document, addresses richer automatically interpretable information; migration and reconstruction remain infrastructure tasks.
why: Missing provenance obstructs reevaluation when standards or detector models change.
key_works: OECD NEA/WPEC Subgroup 50 (2026), *Data-format Requirement Document for an Automatically Readable, Comprehensive and Curated Experimental Reaction Database MEDUSAL*, [publication record](https://gifsymposium2018.gen-4.org/jcms/pl_121852/subgroup-50-data-format-requirement-document-for-an-automatically-readable-comprehensive-and-curated-experimental-reaction-database-medusal).

title: Isotope-resolved origin of the reactor spectral bump
open: Identify the fission isotopes and individual beta branches responsible for the 5-MeV bump, quantitatively reproducing its shape and fuel-evolution dependence. Validate against independent reactor and decay measurements.
status: Reported in the 2010s, the distortion persists despite improved data. The joint PROSPECT–STEREO spectrum finds an excess in 235U, without uniquely identifying the decay branches or other isotopes’ contributions.
why: An explained source spectrum removes a major obstacle to precision neutrino interpretation.
key_works: H. Almazán et al. (2022), *Joint Measurement of the 235U Antineutrino Spectrum by PROSPECT and STEREO*, [arXiv:2107.03371](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03371).

title: Subpercent predictive closure of uranium-235 antineutrino yield
open: Predict absolute 235U antineutrino yield to subpercent accuracy from independent fission and beta-decay data, consistently with direct neutrino and aggregate electron measurements. Resolve remaining normalization differences without fitting the target neutrino yield.
status: The historical flux anomaly motivated renewed work from 2011. Revised summation calculations improve agreement; Perissé et al. (2023) still find incompatibility with legacy aggregate beta spectra and data-dominated uncertainties.
why: Accurate absolute yields strengthen tests of neutrino properties and quantitative reactor monitoring.
key_works: L. Perissé et al. (2023), *A comprehensive revision of the summation method for the prediction of reactor antineutrino fluxes and spectra*, [arXiv:2304.14992](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.14992).

title: Directly isolated uranium-238 antineutrino spectrum
open: Determine the 238U fast-fission antineutrino spectrum with substantially reduced conversion and isotope-mixture dependence, especially at high energy. Require direct isolation or demonstrably identifiable multi-source inference with published covariance.
status: Haag et al. (2014) measured electrons and converted their spectrum, with increasing uncertainty at high energy. A complementary direct-neutrino determination and improved precision remain open.
why: The smaller 238U contribution can still influence the high-energy reactor spectrum.
key_works: N. Haag et al. (2014), *Experimental Determination of the Antineutrino Spectrum of the Fission Products of 238U*, [arXiv:1312.5601](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.5601).

title: Separately constrained plutonium-241 antineutrino spectrum
open: Extract the 241Pu antineutrino spectrum independently of assumed proportionality to 239Pu, including shape and normalization covariance. Demonstrate that correlated fuel evolution cannot substitute another isotope’s change for the inferred signal.
status: Daya Bay’s 2025 full dataset improves aggregate, 235U, and 239Pu spectra. Independent 241Pu extraction remains limited by its smaller contribution and correlated evolution.
why: Separately measuring the fourth major isotope reduces source-model degeneracies across fuel histories.
key_works: F. P. An et al. (2025), *Comprehensive Measurement of the Reactor Antineutrino Spectrum and Flux at Daya Bay*, [arXiv:2501.00746](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.00746).

title: Forbidden beta-shape corrections with measured uncertainties
open: Determine spectral shapes of influential non-unique forbidden fission-product beta transitions from experiment and nuclear-structure calculations. Propagate correlated shape uncertainty into antineutrino predictions and discriminate competing nuclear models.
status: Hayen et al. (2019) showed potentially consequential first-forbidden contributions. Subsequent summation work finds sensitivity to data and modeling choices; assumed allowed shapes do not validate individual transitions.
why: Branch shapes alter antineutrino energies even when total beta intensities are known.
key_works: L. Hayen et al. (2019), *First-forbidden transitions in the reactor anomaly*, [arXiv:1908.08302](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.08302).

title: Reactor antineutrino spectrum below inverse-beta threshold
open: Reconstruct the reactor antineutrino spectrum below approximately 1.8 MeV with calibrated response, background control, and uncertainty independent of assumed summation spectra. Establish which features are identifiable through recoil measurements.
status: Standard inverse-beta measurements cannot access this region. CONUS+ observed reactor coherent scattering in 2025, but an integrated recoil excess does not determine the full subthreshold source spectrum.
why: Exposes a large, weakly tested part of reactor beta-decay emission.
key_works: N. Ackermann et al. (2025), *Direct observation of coherent elastic antineutrino–nucleus scattering*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09322-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09322-2).

title: Remaining eV-scale sterile-neutrino parameter space
open: Test remaining oscillation regions using source-model-independent baseline comparisons and reconcile incompatible claims under shared statistical assumptions. Publish likelihoods for reproducible combinations and systematic-error stress tests.
status: Extensive searches followed the 2011 reactor anomaly. PROSPECT’s final analysis, published in 2025, excludes the Neutrino-4 best-fit point above five sigma; smaller amplitudes and other sterile-neutrino models are not universally excluded.
why: A surviving oscillation signal would establish physics beyond the standard three-neutrino framework.
key_works: M. Andriamirado et al. (2025), *Final Search for Short-Baseline Neutrino Oscillations with the PROSPECT-I Detector at HFIR*, [arXiv:2406.10408](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10408).

title: Precision reactor coherent scattering across target nuclei
open: Measure reactor coherent elastic neutrino–nucleus scattering precisely across different targets, separating weak-interaction physics from recoil response and quenching uncertainty. Require consistency under independent threshold calibrations.
status: CONUS+ reported a 3.7-sigma reactor observation in 2025. Precision cross-target tests and robust separation of detector effects from possible new interactions remain open.
why: Tests weak nuclear charges and possible low-energy interactions while developing compact neutrino detection.
key_works: N. Ackermann et al. (2025), *Direct observation of coherent elastic antineutrino–nucleus scattering*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09322-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09322-2).

title: Tenfold more efficient reactor antineutrino direction finding
open: Proposed moonshot: achieve the same angular uncertainty with at least ten times fewer detected antineutrinos than a specified present detector, retaining a compact deployable instrument. Demonstrate the gain through blinded direction reconstruction.
status: PROSPECT’s directionality measurement, published in 2025, extracted the reactor direction using about 48,000 inverse-beta events. Directionality is demonstrated; information per event and practical deployment remain improvement targets.
why: Efficient direction finding helps distinguish reactor or geophysical neutrino sources.
key_works: M. Andriamirado et al. (2025), *Reactor Antineutrino Directionality Measurement with the PROSPECT-I Detector*, [arXiv:2406.08359](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08359).

title: Validated transfer of the TAO reference spectrum to JUNO
open: Transfer a high-resolution near-reactor spectrum to JUNO with a validated subpercent error budget for core compositions, fuel histories, detector responses, and spectral fine structure. Show that residual source errors cannot mimic targeted oscillation features.
status: Capozzi, Lisi, and Marrone (2020) developed a mapping method; TAO announced first antineutrino measurements in 2026. Demonstrated precision of the complete cross-reactor transfer remains the target.
why: Reliable source transfer strengthens neutrino mass-ordering and precision-oscillation measurements.
key_works: F. Capozzi, E. Lisi, and A. Marrone (2020), *Mapping reactor neutrino spectra from TAO to JUNO*, [arXiv:2006.01648](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.01648); JUNO-TAO (2026), [*First measurement of reactor antineutrinos at JUNO-TAO*](https://indico.cern.ch/event/1522800/contributions/6985955/).

title: Correlation-aware criticality tallies
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Produce local power estimates and confidence intervals that remain calibrated in large, weakly coupled reactor models despite source clustering and population control. Demonstrate coverage across independent calculations, including spatially undersampled regions.
status: A decades-old Monte Carlo difficulty. Fröhlicher et al. demonstrated generational variance reduction on a one-speed slab in 2023; general reactor-scale guarantees remain a research target.
why: Prevents apparently precise calculations from concealing local statistical bias.
key_works: Fröhlicher et al. (2023), *Generational variance reduction in Monte Carlo criticality simulations as a way of mitigating unwanted correlations*, [arXiv:2301.03882](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.03882).

title: Affordable fully transient Monte Carlo
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Reduce computation for continuous-energy, three-dimensional reactor transients by at least tenfold against a declared reference, retaining independently verified time-resolved uncertainty and delayed-neutron dynamics. This is a proposed performance target.
status: Fully transient simulation exists. MC/DC’s 2024 release and 2023 initial-particle sampling methods supply baselines; coupled, long-duration transients remain expensive.
why: Makes independent transient reference solutions practical for routine validation.
key_works: Morgan et al. (2024), *Monte Carlo / Dynamic Code (MC/DC): An accelerated Python package for fully transient neutron transport and rapid methods development*, [DOI:10.21105/joss.06415](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.06415); Variansyah et al. (2023), *An effective initial particle sampling technique for Monte Carlo reactor transient simulations*, [arXiv:2305.07646](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.07646).

title: Positive, conservative adaptive low-rank transport
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Develop adaptive low-rank neutron transport preserving nonnegative flux and particle balance, with usable error bounds through streaming, sharp material interfaces, and transient rank growth.
status: Kusch et al. established a low-rank criticality iteration and simplified convergence analysis in 2022. Savings are demonstrated; the combined guarantees over realistic heterogeneous transients remain unestablished.
why: Reduces memory without sacrificing physically meaningful solutions.
key_works: Kusch, Whewell, McClarren, and Frank (2022), *A low-rank power iteration scheme for neutron transport criticality problems*, [arXiv:2201.12340](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12340).

title: Nonlinear uncertainty through depletion histories
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Propagate correlated nuclear-data, flux, composition, and operating-history uncertainties through repeated irradiation and cooling without uncontrolled linearization. Validate residual-heat and isotope-inventory uncertainty against held-out assays.
status: Diez et al. (2015) showed that approximation choices and covariance libraries materially change burn-up uncertainty. Full sampling supplies a costly baseline; efficient reliable nonlinear propagation remains open.
why: Supports defensible fuel, storage, and waste predictions.
key_works: Diez et al. (2015), *Comparison of nuclear data uncertainty propagation methodologies for PWR burn-up simulations*, [DOI:10.1016/j.anucene.2014.10.022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anucene.2014.10.022).

title: Separating nuclear-data error from model discrepancy
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Determine when reactor measurements can distinguish uncertain nuclear data from thermal-hydraulic closure error, instrumentation bias, and geometric error. Demonstrate identifiable calibration and predictive coverage in a different operating regime.
status: OECD/NEA UAM exercises have developed coupled uncertainty comparisons since the 2000s. Agreement after calibration does not identify which error source was corrected.
why: Avoids compensating errors that fail during extrapolation.
key_works: Avramova et al. (2015), *Multi-physics and multi-scale benchmarking and uncertainty quantification within OECD/NEA framework*, [journal article](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306454914006628).

title: Complete differentiable temperature treatment
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Supply consistent temperature-dependent transport data with verified derivatives and uncertainty across resolved resonances, reaction thresholds, unresolved resonances, and bound-atom scattering. Test feedback derivatives against independent calculations.
status: Windowed multipole methods already provide analytic Doppler broadening in important regimes. The 2021 representation derives derivatives below the first reaction threshold; complete cross-regime consistency remains the target.
why: Enables reliable feedback sensitivities and gradient-based uncertainty analysis.
key_works: Ducru et al. (2021), *Windowed multipole representation of R-matrix cross sections*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevC.103.064610](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevC.103.064610).

title: Homogenization that survives off-reference transients
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Construct reduced reactor models with bounded errors when temperature, control configuration, leakage, and spectra depart from states used to generate homogenized constants. Validate local peaks as well as integral criticality.
status: Superhomogenization and two-step workflows are mature partial solutions. Griffin’s 2024 work demonstrates heterogeneous multiphysics transport as a higher-fidelity reference.
why: Preserves fast calculations without hiding local transient error.
key_works: Wang et al. (2024), *Neutron transport methods for multiphysics heterogeneous reactor core simulation in Griffin*, [DOI:10.1016/j.anucene.2024.110365](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anucene.2024.110365).

title: Portable end-to-end exascale reactor simulation
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Retain high parallel efficiency across different accelerators for complete depletion–transport–thermal-fluid workflows, including data movement, tallies, coupling, and uncertainty estimation. Publish reproducible performance at fixed physical error.
status: ExaSMR demonstrated major GPU and coupled-code advances. Isolated kernel throughput or projected machine-scale rates do not establish complete-workflow portability.
why: Makes large simulations affordable and reproducible across computing facilities.
key_works: ORNL, [*ExaSMR: Coupled Monte Carlo Neutronics and Fluid Flow Simulation of Small Modular Reactors*](https://www.ornl.gov/project/exasmr-coupled-monte-carlo-neutronics-and-fluid-flow-simulation-small-modular-reactors); Romano et al. (2015), *OpenMC*, [DOI:10.1016/j.anucene.2014.07.048](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anucene.2014.07.048).

title: Reactor surrogate validity outside training conditions
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Establish when a learned reactor surrogate must abstain because temperature, geometry, composition, or accident trajectory lies outside validated support. Measure error-detection failures on deliberately withheld physical regimes.
status: Learned surrogates are widely demonstrated. NEA’s EGMUP task force organizes trustworthy-AI benchmarking; universal extrapolation assurance remains unavailable.
why: Prevents fast predictions from silently replacing justified physical estimates.
key_works: OECD/NEA, *Expert Group on Reactor Systems Multi-Physics*, [active programme, accessed 2026](https://www.oecdnea.org/jcms/pl_32479/expert-group-on-reactor-systems-multi-physics-egmup).

title: Blind multiphysics reactor benchmark suites
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Create independently administered benchmarks with withheld operating states, local measurements, correlated uncertainties, and complete scoring rules. Test prediction before participants tune to the answers.
status: The TVA Watts Bar benchmark launched in 2019 and preserves valuable plant evidence. An extensive openly reproducible blind suite spanning reactor families remains an infrastructure target.
why: Measures predictive transfer rather than fit to familiar cases.
key_works: OECD/NEA (2019–), [*TVA Watts Bar Unit 1 Multi-Physics Benchmark*](https://oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_32202/tva-watts-bar-unit-1-multi-physics-benchmark).

title: Honest effective sample size for integral benchmarks
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Quantify how shared facilities, instruments, materials, and evaluation assumptions reduce independent information in benchmark collections. Propagate dependencies into validation margins outside the experimental envelope.
status: Integral benchmark programmes provide extensive evaluated cases and uncertainty descriptions. Many nominal cases do not automatically supply equivalent independent evidence.
why: Avoids overstating validation strength for novel fuels and geometries.
key_works: OECD/NEA, [*International Criticality Safety Benchmark Evaluation Project*](https://oecd-nea.org/jcms/pl_24498/international-criticality-safety-benchmark-evaluation-project-icsbep); Diez et al. (2015), *Comparison of nuclear data uncertainty propagation methodologies*, [DOI:10.1016/j.anucene.2014.10.022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anucene.2014.10.022).

title: Experimental validation of moving delayed-neutron precursors
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Validate spatial precursor transport and decay for modern circulating-fuel geometries and operating envelopes using independent flow and time-dependent neutron measurements. Resolve when reduced kinetics remains accurate as circulation changes.
status: Historical molten-salt experiments provide partial validation. Griffin–Pronghorn passed a CNRS numerical benchmark in 2024; numerical agreement does not establish experimental coverage of modern designs.
why: Constrains dynamic feedback in liquid-fuel reactors.
key_works: Jaradat, Choi, and Abou-Jaoude (2024), *Verification of Griffin-Pronghorn-Coupled Multiphysics Code System Against CNRS Molten Salt Reactor Benchmark*, [DOI:10.1080/00295639.2024.2306702](https://doi.org/10.1080/00295639.2024.2306702).

title: Identifiability limits of neutron-noise diagnosis
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Characterize combinations of core vibration, coolant fluctuations, and detector drift that are indistinguishable from a finite noisy detector set. Prove bounds or construct experiments separating ambiguous causes.
status: CORTEX developed methods and controlled-reactor experiments during 2017–2021. The requested identifiability map is a proposed extension, rather than an existing named theorem.
why: Establishes when localization is supported by evidence and when additional sensors are needed.
key_works: Demazière et al. (2017), [*Noise-based core monitoring and diagnostics—Overview of the CORTEX project*](https://research.chalmers.se/en/publication/253656).

title: Certified sensitivities for moving reactor geometry
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Compute stable gradients and error estimates for coupled transients when deformation changes geometry and transport simultaneously. Verify derivatives against independent perturbations through nonlinear thermal expansion and feedback.
status: GeN-Foam has coupled neutronics, thermal hydraulics, and deformation since 2015. Coupled simulation does not itself provide a general certificate of derivative accuracy.
why: Makes sensitivity-based design and uncertainty calculations trustworthy.
key_works: Fiorina et al. (2015), *GeN-Foam: a novel OpenFOAM-based multi-physics solver for 2D/3D transient analysis of nuclear reactors*, [DOI:10.1016/j.nucengdes.2015.05.035](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nucengdes.2015.05.035).

title: Reproducible digital evidence across a plant lifetime
subfield: Reactor physics, transport, and computational verification
open: Preserve executable links among requirements, as-built geometry, material provenance, simulation inputs, inspection findings, and modifications. Demonstrate independent reconstruction of past calculations after software and supplier changes.
status: INL’s 2024 digital-engineering implementations demonstrate linked models and workflows. Durable interoperable evidence across decades and organizations remains a deployment problem.
why: Reduces repeated qualification and prevents undocumented model drift.
key_works: Finan, Ritter, Suyderhoud, and Marshall (2024), *Digital engineering implementation in nuclear demonstration and nonproliferation projects at Idaho National Laboratory*, [DOI:10.3389/fenrg.2024.1443896](https://doi.org/10.3389/fenrg.2024.1443896).

title: Origin of bimodal intragranular gas bubbles
open: Determine which combination of nucleation, dislocation trapping, coalescence, and irradiation-driven gas removal creates the two observed nanometre-scale bubble populations in UO₂. Predict both distributions across temperature and fission rate without separately fitting each irradiation.
status: A decades-old microstructure question. A 2025 phase-field study reproduced bimodality using gas re-solution, but alternative mechanisms remain experimentally distinguishable.
why: Bubble populations control swelling, gas retention, and subsequent fragmentation.
key_works: Jiajun Zhao et al. (2025), *Mesoscale simulation on bimodal distribution of nano-sized intragranular fission bubbles in UO₂*, [journal article](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0167577X24019591).

title: Fission-spike gas re-solution law
open: Establish a transferable rate law for fission-fragment tracks returning xenon from bubbles to the fuel matrix, including bubble size, track offset, energy deposition, and nearby dislocations. Use independent gas inventories to distinguish thermal-spike and ballistic mechanisms.
status: Setyawan et al. parameterized atomistic re-solution in 2018. Conversion of electronic deposition into atomic heating remains a source of uncertainty in engineering-scale rates.
why: Incorrect re-solution rates propagate into swelling and gas-release predictions.
key_works: W. Setyawan et al. (2018), *Atomistic model of xenon gas bubble re-solution rate due to thermal spike in uranium oxide*, [DOI:10.1063/1.5042770](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.5042770).

title: Gas escape through evolving grain-boundary networks
open: Predict when a three-dimensional grain-boundary bubble network connects to an external fuel surface while boundaries move. Simultaneously predict boundary coverage, connected paths, and release histories across grain-size distributions.
status: Chatterjee et al.’s 2025 preprint couples cluster dynamics and phase fields in large three-dimensional polycrystals. Independent validation of the resulting release laws remains open.
why: Connectivity, rather than total porosity alone, determines when retained gas escapes.
